paras: The Lancaster riot of 1882 was a shooting on 27 September 1882 in the main street of Lancaster, South Carolina, in which armed white men killed at least four Black men from a mounted procession after a political meeting addressed by the Independent congressional candidate E. B. C. Cash. Reported deaths rose from four to as many as twelve, while no white man was said to have been seriously hurt. Southern Democratic papers called the shooting self-defense against a drunken mob, whereas Northern Republican voices called it a massacre and political murder.

Cash, endorsed by Republicans and Greenbackers, spoke at a mass meeting at Lancaster Court House to a crowd that the News and Courier's correspondent put at about 700 Black men. According to an eye-witness account printed in Charlotte, the meeting was held in a grove about a quarter mile from town with F. A. Clinton, a Black man, presiding. When D. J. Carter, editor of the Lancaster Ledger, rose to reply to Cash, a crowd broke down the stand and dragged him and other white Democrats off it, and Clinton and other Black men protected them. Cash went to his hotel room and stayed there through the trouble.

Later that afternoon, as the sheriff was jailing a drunken Black man, named by one account as Hamp Mabley, a mounted procession led by William Crockett rode up Main street. In the Democratic accounts Crockett pointed out a white man, named by Charlotte sources as J. Quay Dunovant of Chester, as the man who had done the shooting and fired at him, the ball striking a memorandum book. The Charlotte Observer instead reported that he only aimed, and that 'His finger never pulled the trigger' before a white man shot him dead.

After Crockett fell from his horse, firing became general, and whites who had already armed themselves fired on the crowd, killing Thomas Cunningham and Nathan Cureton outright. Mack Mobley died of his wounds the next day, and Ransom Brown, Joseph Foster and William Cureton were badly wounded, along with eight or ten others hurt slightly. Mules were killed, and buildings near the scene were riddled with bullets and buckshot.

The Black horsemen withdrew to another part of town, and the town intendant telegraphed Chester for aid while word went into the country for white men to arm and come to town. State Senator Giles J. Patterson asked Governor Hagood to send the Lee Light Infantry, but the order was countermanded once quiet returned.

Coroner Beldon held an inquest, and the jury found that the dead came to their deaths 'at the hands of parties unknown to the jury'. The Union Times printed testimony by Mobley's wife that he had said before dying that the whites were not to blame. No report of an arrest of any white man, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

A week later a Charlotte dispatch said white residents were picketing the town for fear it would be burned and that the death toll had reached twelve. Quoting the Lancaster Review, Chandler reported that whites had organized a military company, the Lancaster Greys, and drilled with state arms.

The first wires ran across the country on 29 and 30 September under headlines such as 'FOUR NEGROES KILLED' and 'RIOT AT A POLITICAL MEETING', and many stressed that Cash had killed a man in a duel. South Carolina and Charlotte papers blamed whiskey and Cash's speech, the Abbeville Press and Banner heading its report 'THE POOR BLACKS AGAIN THE VICTIMS OF EVIL TEACHING'. The Charlotte Observer judged that 'The whites acted in self-defense', and the Union Times used the deaths in an editorial warning Black voters against Greenback leaders who left 'the deluded colored men to be shot at like targets'.

A Richmond dispatch carried in the North under the headline 'THE MASSACRE' reported seven dead and said Cash had hidden 'to escape the fury of the whites'. The Chicago Tribune, reprinted in Ohio and Wisconsin, wrote that Red Shirts had lain in wait and renewed the attack, killing six. In November, Secretary W. E. Chandler's letter to the New-York Tribune named the four dead as 'colored Republicans' killed in 'political murders' meant to suppress the county's Republican vote.

Accounts differ on who started the shooting: the wires and the News and Courier said Crockett fired first, the Charlotte Observer said he never fired, and the Greenville News said a Black man had been shot in the first quarrel. Reported deaths ranged from four to twelve and the wounded from three to twenty-eight, while only four of the dead are named. Chandler's letter dated the riot 27 October, a month later than every dispatch.

reader.title: Lancaster riot of 1882
bases: Armed white townsmen fired on a mounted Black crowd in Lancaster's main street after a Greenback-Independent meeting, killing four or more Black men while no white was seriously hurt (A4, A7, A23).

Wire, News and Courier, Charlotte Observer, Greenville News and eye-witness accounts agree that at least four Black men were killed in Lancaster on 27 September 1882, though they differ on who started it and on the toll (A3, A14, A22, A23).

accounts.label: First Lancaster wire / Columbia special
accounts.gist: A white Democrat was struck at the stand; later about 100 mounted, armed Black men led by Crockett rode through town, Crockett fired at a white man, was shot dead, and general firing killed three more.

accounts.label: News and Courier correspondent
accounts.gist: Drinking Black men dragged Carter off the stand; after the sheriff jailed a drunk man, a procession of about 200 under William Crockett came up, Crockett fired from his horse, and 'peaceable citizens' quelled the fight; four or five killed.

accounts.label: Charlotte Observer
accounts.gist: A drunken Black man aimed a pistol at Dunnivan in the hotel door but never pulled the trigger before a white man shot him dead; whites who had 'fully armed themselves' returned fire; four dead, three wounded, no whites hurt.

accounts.label: Eye-witness account (Charlotte Home and Democrat)
accounts.gist: A Black mob tore down the stand and beat the white Democrats; later Crockett fired at Dunovant, his ball striking a memorandum book, and was shot from his saddle; three killed outright, twenty or thirty wounded, later seven or eight dead.

accounts.label: Greenville Daily News special
accounts.gist: A Black man was shot in the first difficulty; a crowd of Black men then pointed out the white man they blamed, and a pitched battle killed four colored men.

accounts.label: Richmond private information
accounts.gist: Seven killed and twenty-one wounded; Cash hid from 'the fury of the whites'; a mounted force fired over the heads of rioting whites into the Black men; whites justified it by a claimed plot to burn the town.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune / W. E. Chandler (Republican)
accounts.gist: Red Shirts attacked the Black crowd after Cash left, lay in wait and renewed the attack; moderate Democrats were said to state the disturbance was organized in advance.

framing.detail: The Charlotte Observer called it 'a regular drunken row' in which the whites 'acted in self-defense'.
The Abbeville Press and Banner headlined 'THE POOR BLACKS AGAIN THE VICTIMS OF EVIL TEACHING' and said the Black crowd tried 'to Take the Town'.
The Union Times ran it under 'Bloody Work of Greenbackers' and blamed demagogues who left 'deluded colored men' to be shot.
Northern dailies ran the Lancaster and Columbia wires under 'FOUR NEGROES KILLED' and 'RIOT AT A POLITICAL MEETING', stressing Cash the 'Duellist'.
The Portland Daily Press headlined the Richmond report 'THE MASSACRE'.
The Chicago Tribune editorial and Chandler's letter called it a Red Shirt massacre and 'political murders' meant to suppress the Republican vote.

conflicts.note: Only four dead are named (A24, A29); later counts add men who died of wounds and cannot be checked against names.
All agree no white was seriously hurt in the street fight; Carter and a white Democrat were struck at the stand.
